restatements.text: Requires individuals keeping a firearm in a residence to store it in a locked container when it is not being carried or used.
Directs the Department to issue a storage certificate to applicants who pay a $25 fee.
Preempts local governments from adopting or enforcing their own ordinances regarding firearm storage, occupying the field exclusively at the state level.

analysis.answer: Current law does not govern residential firearm storage at the state level but allows cities and counties to enact their own ordinances. The proposed measure imposes a statewide requirement that residential firearms be stored in locked containers when not in use, creates a $25 storage certificate, and entirely preempts local governments from adopting or enforcing their own firearm storage rules.

Applicants for a storage certificate will pay a $25 fee. Gun owners will bear the compliance costs of purchasing safes or lockboxes. The state will incur administrative costs to process certificate applications, which may be offset by the collected fees.

Gun owners pay the costs of purchasing locked containers and the certificate fee if they apply. Companies that manufacture and sell gun safes will financially benefit from increased demand. Household members, especially children, and the broader community may benefit from a reduced risk of accidental shootings and firearm theft.

Many gun owners will purchase lockboxes, increasing sales for retailers. Some may ignore the mandate due to the difficulty of enforcing a rule inside private homes. Local governments will cease enforcing any existing local storage laws. The state agency responsible will have to design and administer a system for issuing storage certificates.

The measure addresses unauthorized access to firearms at home (e.g., accidents involving children or gun theft) by mandating locked storage, and it removes the complexity of inconsistent local laws by preempting them. The storage mandate's effectiveness is constrained by the inherent difficulty of proactive enforcement in private residences. Furthermore, the text requires the issuance of a storage certificate but asserts no explicit requirement to obtain one, leaving that mechanism disconnected from the mandate.

The state government, specifically the unnamed 'Department,' gains exclusive regulatory and administrative power over residential firearm storage. Local city and county governments lose their authority to regulate in this policy area.

The effect is debated. Public health researchers generally find that safe storage laws reduce the rates of accidental shootings and youth suicides. However, some researchers argue that mandating locked storage can impede a homeowner's ability to quickly access a firearm for self-defense during a home invasion.

Enforcement of the storage mandate will be difficult and costly to proactively administer within private homes, meaning enforcement will likely be reactive, occurring only after an incident such as a theft or accidental shooting. Processing storage certificates will involve routine administrative friction for both applicants and the state.
As a statutory measure, it can be amended or repealed by the state legislature, subject to ordinary legislative thresholds and procedures.
